items.title: Your blood vessels stretched end to end would circle Earth twice
items.claim: The human body contains about 100,000 kilometres of blood vessels, almost all of which is capillaries. Earth's equator is 40,075 km. Two and a half wraps.
items.prompt: How is so much vessel length packed inside a person?

options.text: Capillaries are ~5-10 micrometres in diameter — they pass red blood cells in single file. Their tiny cross-section means enormous total length fits in tissue, while still leaving most tissue volume for cells
Vessels run in spirals to fit

items.reveal:
Aorta: ~2.5 cm diameter, 1 metre long. Branches into arteries, arterioles, then capillaries. Capillaries number ~10 billion in the body, total length ~80,000-100,000 km.

Almost every cell is within ~50 micrometres of a capillary — the maximum diffusion distance for oxygen. This drives the geometry: dense, thin, ramifying vessels.

Total cross-sectional area increases at each branching level: aorta ~5 cm^2, all capillaries combined ~4000 cm^2. By the conservation equation (flow = velocity * area), blood velocity drops from ~30 cm/s in the aorta to ~0.1 cm/s in capillaries — allowing time for diffusion.

Vascular networks follow allometric scaling laws (West, Brown, Enquist) that approximate optimal transport — minimising energy cost of moving blood. The same scaling rules describe trees, river networks, urban roads.

New capillary formation (angiogenesis) is closely controlled. Tumours hijack it to grow blood supply; anti-angiogenic drugs (bevacizumab) starve them.
items.why: A circulatory system 100,000 km long sounds external. It's packed inside a human body because each capillary is a fraction of a hair wide — and there are billions of them.

items.title: Your blood sugar is regulated within a 30% range despite irregular meals
items.claim: Normal fasting blood glucose: 4-6 mmol/L. After a meal: rises to 7-8, then back to baseline within 2 hours. Healthy people maintain this range whether they eat constantly or fast for a day.

options.text: Insulin (from pancreatic beta cells) lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and storage; glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it by mobilising stored glycogen — a classic antagonistic pair under negative feedback

items.reveal:
After a meal: blood glucose rises. Beta cells in the pancreas detect it via glucokinase and secrete insulin. Insulin tells muscle and fat to take up glucose, and the liver to store it as glycogen.

Between meals: glucose drops. Alpha cells secrete glucagon. Glucagon tells the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood. If glycogen runs out (after ~24 hours fasting), gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol takes over.

Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune destruction of beta cells. No insulin. Blood glucose unregulated. Discovered to be treatable with injected insulin by Banting and Best (1921, Nobel 1923) — life expectancy of Type 1 patients went from months to decades within a year of insulin's availability.

Type 2 diabetes: insulin RESISTANCE develops in target tissues. Beta cells initially compensate (more insulin) then eventually fail. Affects ~10% of adults globally. Strongly linked to obesity and inactivity.

The brain is unique in burning glucose nearly exclusively (~120 g/day, 20% of total body glucose use) — which is why hypoglycaemia causes confusion, seizures and unconsciousness within minutes.
items.why: Hormones feel like signals from somewhere distant. In glucose regulation, two opposing hormones from the same gland keep blood sugar within a tight band — a textbook example of antagonistic negative feedback.

items.title: Plants bend toward light by growing more on the dark side
items.claim: A potted plant on a windowsill tilts toward the window within hours. It doesn't push or twist — it grows ASYMMETRICALLY. Cells on the shaded side elongate faster than cells on the lit side, bending the stem toward the light.

options.text: Auxin (indole-3-acetic acid) accumulates on the shaded side and stimulates cell elongation; this differential auxin distribution was demonstrated by Frits Went and Charles Darwin in classic shoot-tip experiments
Water collects on the dark side
Light evaporates cells on the lit side

items.reveal_title: Darwin's coleoptiles to Went's agar blocks
items.reveal:
Charles Darwin (1880, 'The Power of Movement in Plants', with son Francis) showed that the tip of a grass coleoptile senses light, but the bending occurs lower down — implying a signal travels.

Boysen-Jensen (1913) showed a thin agar block between the tip and the bending region allows the signal through; mica does not. The signal is chemical.

Frits Went (1928) collected the signal in agar blocks and applied it asymmetrically to decapitated coleoptiles, causing bending. The substance was named auxin (Greek auxein, 'to grow').

Mechanism: blue light receptors (phototropins) on the lit side trigger redistribution of PIN auxin efflux carriers. Auxin pumps preferentially to the shaded side. Higher auxin there causes cell wall loosening (expansin proteins) and elongation. The stem bends.

Auxin's reach extends beyond phototropism: apical dominance (shoot tip suppresses lateral buds), root gravitropism (concentrations bend roots DOWN), fruit development, leaf abscission, callus formation in tissue culture. It's the master plant hormone.
items.why: Plant movement seems passive. Phototropism is an active, hormonal, asymmetric growth response — controlled by a single small molecule with effects across the whole plant's life cycle.
